# A Simple and General Approach to top-_k_ Selection Motti Goldberger
Yale School of Management, motti.goldberger@yale.edu
Nils Rudi
Yale School of Management, nils.rudi@yale.edu **Abstract.** This paper considers the Bayesian top-_k_ identification problem, wherein a decision maker is tasked with selecting _k_ items from a pool of items of unknown quality. To assess the items, the decision maker adaptively allocates a fixed sampling budget, where each sample of an item yields a noisy observation of its quality, with the objective of minimizing the expected opportunity cost of the selected set. We propose an approach that allocates each batch of samples by minimizing a surrogate objective derived from an upper bound on the expected opportunity cost. The approach is general: samples can be allocated in batches, the selection size _k_ is arbitrary, and it applies to many sampling distributions. It is also simple and intuitive. We prove that the method’s posterior expected opportunity cost decays at an exponential rate of at least half the best rate achievable by any sampling rule. In simulations across a wide range of settings, the method is competitive with, and often improves upon, the best existing algorithm in each setting. **Key words:** Ranking-and-Selection, Best-Arm Identification, Top-_k_ Identification ### 1. Introduction This paper studies the problem of a decision maker who faces a large pool of items with unknown quality, can assess them through noisy and costly samples, and wants to identify and select the best item(s). This is commonly referred to as a _ranking and selection_ task in the operations literature (Chen et al. 2000, Chen and Lee 2010, Hong et al. 2021), and as a _best-arm(s) identification_ task in the multi-armed bandit literature (Kalyanakrishnan et al. 2012, Kaufmann et al. 2016, Russo 2020). This problem arises in many domains, including clinical trials (Villar et al. 2015, Chick et al. 2022), A/B/n testing (Scott 2015, Ju et al. 2019), machine-learning model selection and hyperparameter optimization (Snoek et al. 2012, Jamieson and Talwalkar 2016, Li et al. 2018), and simulation optimization (Fu et al. 2005). In each setting, the key question is how to adaptively allocate a fixed sampling budget to maximize the quality of the final selection. A central goal of this paper is to treat the problem with generality so that the method is useful across a range of settings. Two aspects of this generality are worth discussing up front. The first concerns how samples are collected. The most adaptive option is to allocate one sample at a time and wait to observe the outcome before choosing the next. However, this can be impractical to implement. For example, in clinical trials, one may not be able to wait to observe an outcome before assigning the next treatment (Robertson et al. 2023), and in simulation optimization, many simulations may be run in parallel (Hong et al. 2021). We therefore consider the partially adaptive case, in which _batches_ of samples are chosen in rounds, and outcomes are observed between rounds. The second aspect is the target number of items to select. Choosing the single best one (_k_=1) is the most common and most studied case, but some of the applications above instead call

<tbc>for selecting several items. Our method can handle any target selection size _k_, giving it a wider range of applicability.

There are two common metrics for how "good" a sample allocation procedure is. One is its probability of correct selection (PCS), the probability that the selected items are the true best items (Chen et al. 2000, Glynn and Juneja 2004, Li et al. 2025). The other is its expected opportunity cost (EOC), sometimes referred to as simple regret, which is the expected shortfall in value between the selected set and the true best set (Chick and Inoue 2001, Gao and Chen 2015). PCS treats every incorrect selection equally, while EOC makes bigger mistakes more costly. For many tasks, EOC, which we adopt as our objective, is the more natural fit since a big mistake can be far worse than a marginal one. That said, the two are closely related. In simulations, a method that performs well on one metric tends to perform well on the other, and our theoretical guarantees apply to both objectives.

Given the objective, the decision maker’s problem can be formulated as a finite-horizon dynamic program. In each round, given the current state (the posterior distribution over item values) and the available budget, one chooses the optimal batch of samples by accounting for all possible outcomes and future states. However, the complexity of this program grows rapidly with the budget size, so solving it exactly is out of reach (Frazier et al. 2008, Hong et al. 2021, Zhang et al. 2023). This has motivated a large body of literature, which we group into two broad categories. The first set of methods allocates samples by solving a sequence of static optimization problems, one per round, in place of the dynamic program. The second group constructs allocation rules directly from the current state without solving an optimization problem. We take the first approach and construct a per-round surrogate objective whose minimizer gives the sample allocation.

There are several ways to form a sequence of one-round static objectives. In a Bayesian formulation, one common approach is to maximize the expected value of information (EVI), the improvement in the quality of the final selection that collecting the next batch would produce (Chick and Inoue 2001, Chick et al. 2010). When samples follow a Gaussian distribution and are chosen one at a time, Frazier et al. (2008, 2009) show that this can be computed exactly for the top-1 EOC objective, yielding the knowledge gradient (KG) policy. In general, however, even the one-step look-ahead objective is intractable, so the literature resorts to approximations. Examples targeting PCS include AOAP for top-1 identification (Peng et al. 2018), and AOAm (Zhang et al. 2023) and EMIp (Liu et al. 2024) for top-_k_, all designed for Gaussian samples. For AOAm, Zhang et al. (2023) also prove that the sampling proportions converge to the proportions that maximize the asymptotic error-decay rate, assuming their necessary sample-proportion conditions have a unique solution.

A second approach in this category, referred to as optimal computing budget allocation (OCBA) (Chen and Lee 2010), assumes that in each round the current estimates of the means are the true means and finds the sample allocation that would be optimal under this assumption (Chen et al. 2000). However, even with this assumption, the problem is generally intractable. It is therefore commonly approached by constructing a bound on the objective, a lower bound for PCS or an upper bound for EOC, and deriving allocations that<tbc>

<tbc>optimize the bound as the budget goes to infinity. Most of this work concerns Gaussian samples and top-1 selection under PCS, with extensions to top-_k_ (Chen et al. 2008, Gao and Chen 2016), and to top-1 and top-_k_ selection under EOC (He et al. 2007, Gao and Chen 2015).

An alternative approach targets learning the allocation that maximizes the exponential rate at which the probability of incorrect selection decays as the budget grows, the large-deviation rate (Glynn and Juneja 2004). Algorithms of this kind run sequentially, again treating the current mean estimates as the truth, and choose allocations using the optimality conditions for this rate. Chen and Ryzhov (2023) establish such an algorithm that applies to general distributions in the _k_=1 setting and prove that the sampling proportions converge to the optimal proportions as the budget approaches infinity.

Next, we review methods that construct sampling rules directly from the current state. Methods similar in spirit to our approach are confidence and gap-based frequentist approaches, which allocate samples based on how close items are to the current estimated top-_k_ cutoff and how uncertain their estimated values are, such as gap-e (Gabillon et al. 2011, Bubeck et al. 2013) and KL-LUCB (Kaufmann and Kalyanakrishnan 2013). Our allocation algorithm is based on the same two quantities, but differs in how the top-_k_ cutoff is defined, how the distance from it is measured, and how uncertainty is used.

Elimination algorithms (Audibert et al. 2010, Karnin et al. 2013) divide sampling into rounds, allocate samples uniformly among the remaining items within a round, and eliminate the empirically weakest items according to an elimination schedule. The successive accepts and rejects (SAR) approach (Bubeck et al. 2013) also "accepts" empirically strong items, avoiding spending samples on items already determined to likely be in the top-_k_.

Algorithms based on the expected improvement (EI) rule, which originates from the Bayesian optimization literature (Jones et al. 1998), have been designed for top-1 selection problems (Ryzhov 2016, Qin et al. 2017, Chen and Ryzhov 2019). For each item, the algorithm computes the expected amount by which the item’s value exceeds that of the current best item, and samples the item with the largest improvement score. In the Gaussian case, Chen and Ryzhov (2019) show that a variant of EI achieves the optimal sampling proportions asymptotically.

A family of Bayesian algorithms referred to as _top two_ algorithms allocates a sample in each round by identifying a "leader" item and a "challenger" item, then flipping a weighted coin to decide which of the two to sample (Russo 2020). Various methods have been proposed for choosing the leader and challenger (Jourdan et al. 2022), for example, based on Thompson sampling (Russo 2020) or expected improvement scores (Qin et al. 2017). For _k_=1 and a broad class of sampling distributions, Russo (2020) proves that with an unbiased coin, the posterior probability of an incorrect selection decays at an exponential rate of at least half the best achievable rate. Russo (2020) further shows that with suitable tuning of the coin flip probability, it attains the optimal decay rate. Qin et al. (2017) establish the corresponding results for top two expected improvement with Gaussian samples. You et al. (2023) and Qin and You (2026) extend top<tbc>

<tbc>two methods to the top-_k_ setting and give a rigorous way to weight the coin such that in the top-1 Gaussian setting, the posterior probability of an incorrect selection decays at the optimal exponential rate without a tuning parameter, though their general top-_k_ sampling rules do not come with posterior error decay rate guarantees. Establishing optimality for general _k_ is more difficult because the conditions governing how samples must be allocated among items have a more complicated structure (Zhang et al. 2023, Qin and You 2026). Russo (2020) conjectures that his top-_k_ extension of top two Thompson sampling achieves a posterior error decay rate of at least half the optimum.

Given the rich literature on this problem, our motivation for this work stems from a related project. In Goldberger and Rudi (2026), we study the top-_k_ identification problem in a _different_ setting with three key components that existing methods do not address in combination. First, the decision maker can choose among different binary sample forms (in particular, a binary rating of an item or a comparison of two items), each with a different cost and signal quality. Methods that allocate directly from the current state have no clear way to handle this, whereas methods that solve a static problem may, because the costs and signal quality of each sample form can be incorporated into the objective. Second, that paper considers "small" budget settings, so analysis in the asymptotic regime is not of primary importance. Third, samples may be collected in batches. Among the methods above, OCBA-style and elimination-based algorithms support batching (Jun et al. 2016). However, OCBA algorithms generally rely on asymptotic analysis, and elimination-based algorithms are often outperformed in simulation by other methods such as gap-e and KL-LUCB (Bubeck et al. 2013, Kaufmann and Kalyanakrishnan 2013, Zhang et al. 2023). This motivated us to develop a new method for that specific problem. In this paper, building on insights from that work, we develop a simpler, far more general method for Bayesian top-_k_ identification.

**Our approach.** We take the approach of solving a sequence of tractable static optimization problems, which we develop in two steps. First, we give an upper bound on EOC, structurally different from those in the OCBA literature on EOC, and discuss why this structure has the potential for an improved algorithm. Second, to address the intractability of minimizing this bound as a one-round static problem, we approximate the future posterior distribution after a batch via expected moment matching rather than relying on asymptotic analysis. This idea originates in the EVI and OCBA literature with Gaussian samples by Chen et al. (1997), He et al. (2007), and Zhang et al. (2023), and we generalize it to other distributions. These two steps yield a simple, interpretable per-round static surrogate objective. A key property of the surrogate is that it is separable across items, enabling efficient algorithms for solving the batch problem without relying on heuristics.

**Results and theoretical guarantees.** Similar to the top two and modified expected-improvement methods for _k_=1, our method is conceptually simple and intuitive, yet remarkably comes with strong theoretical performance guarantees for general _k_. For a broad class of sampling distributions, we prove that posterior EOC (as well as the posterior probability of an incorrect selection) decays at an exponential rate of at least<tbc>

<tbc>half the best achievable rate. This establishes the type of general-_k_ guarantee conjectured by Russo (2020), but for our sampling rule.

In a range of simulations, we demonstrate that our method is competitive with and often improves on the current state-of-the-art approaches, including those specialized to _k_=1 as well as those for general _k\>_1, those specialized to Gaussian as well as other distributions, and both at small and large budgets. These comparisons are conducted in the non-batched setting to include as many existing methods as possible. In the batched setting, we show that our method significantly outperforms existing batch algorithms and its performance degrades less as the batch size grows.

We believe this method can be valuable to both researchers and practitioners. It is flexible across a wide range of practical settings, is competitive with the best algorithms in each of these settings, and extends naturally to richer settings, such as those with varying sample forms and sampling costs.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: §2 formulates the model and objective, §3 derives the surrogate objective and the batch allocation algorithm, §4 establishes the theoretical guarantees, §5 presents the numerical experiments, and §6 concludes.

**2. Model and objective**

We consider _I_ items, indexed _i_=1_,...,I_, each with an unknown mean \(\theta_i\in\mathcal{J}\) , where \(\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is an open interval. The goal is to select the _k\<I_ items with the largest means. Each item _i_ has a prior distribution \(\Pi_{i,0}\) on \(\theta_i\) with density \(\pi_{i,0}\). For item _i_, let Y_<sub>i</sub>_ be the outcome space, and let \(\{P_i(\cdot|\theta):\theta\in\mathcal{J}\}\) be a known mean-parametrized family of distributions on Y_<sub>i</sub>_ with density or mass function \(p_i(\cdot|\theta)\). Conditional on \(\theta_i\), the _n_th observation _Y<sub>i,n</sub>_ from item _i_ is drawn i.i.d. from \(P_i(\cdot|\theta_i)\), with \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{i,n}|\theta_i]=\theta_i\). We make the following regularity assumption.

ASSUMPTION 1 **(Regular one-parameter Bayesian model)**. _For each i_=1_,...,I, the prior_ \(\Pi_{i,0}\) _and sampling family_ \(\{P_i(\cdot|\theta):\theta\in\mathcal{J}\}\) _are such that for every_ \(n\ge 0\) _and every_ \((y_1,\dots,y_n)\in\mathcal{Y}_i^n\) _the posterior of_ \(\theta_i\) _conditioned on_ {_Y_<sub>_i,_1</sub>=_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,Y<sub>i,n</sub>=y<sub>n</sub>_} _has continuous positive density on_ J _and finite second moment, and the corresponding posterior predictive distribution of Y_<sub>_i,n_+1</sub> _has finite second moment. In addition, the priors and observations are independent across items._

Remark 1 gives examples of standard conjugate pairs (ESCP) satisfying Assumption 1 that we will refer to throughout the paper.

REMARK 1 (ESCP). _ESCP covered by Assumption 1:_

- _Gaussian:_ \(Y_{i,n}|\theta_i\sim N(\theta_i,\sigma_i^2)\) _with_ \(\sigma_i^2\) _known, prior_ \(\theta_i\sim N(m_i(0),s_i^2(0)),\mathcal{J}=\mathbb{R}\).<tbc>

**-** _Bernoulli:_ \(Y_{i,n}|\theta_i\sim\text{Bern}(\theta_i),\text{\textit{prior}}\theta_i\sim\text{Beta}(a_i(0),b_i(0)),\mathcal{J}=(0,1)\).<tbc>

**-** _Poisson:_ \(Y_{i,n}|\theta_i\sim\text{Pois}(\theta_i),\text{\textit{prior}}\theta_i\sim\text{Gamma}(a_i(0),b_i(0))\) _with rate_ \(b_i(0),\mathcal{J}=(0,\infty)\).<tbc>

- _Gamma with known shape:_ \(Y_{i,n}|\theta_i\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\kappa_i,\theta_i/\kappa_i)\) _with scale_ \(\theta_i/\kappa_i\) _and_ \(\kappa_i\) _known (_\(\kappa_i=1\) _gives the exponential distribution), prior_ \(\theta_i\sim\mathrm{InvGamma}(a_i(0),b_i(0))\) _with a<sub>i</sub>_(0)_\>_2, \(b_i(0)>0,\mathcal{J}=(0,\infty)\).<tbc>

**-** _Lognormal with known log-variance:_ \(Y_{i,n}|\theta_i\sim\mathrm{Lognormal}(\mathrm{log}\theta_i-\sigma_i^2/2\), \(\sigma_i^2)\) _with_ \(\sigma_i^2\) _known, prior_ \(\mathrm{log}\theta_i\sim N(m_i(0),s_i^2(0)),\mathcal{J}=(0,\infty)\).

Sampling proceeds in _T_+1 rounds, an optional warm-up round indexed _t_=0 followed by _T_ adaptive rounds. In the warm-up round, each item is sampled \(n_0\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) times. In rounds _t_=1_,...,T_, we choose a batch of \(B_t\in\mathbb{Z}_+\) samples, where the per-round batch sizes \(\{B_t\}_{t=1}^T\) are pre-specified. The choice of samples in round _t_ is denoted by the vector \(\Delta^t=(\Delta_1^t,\dots,\Delta_I^t)\), where \(\Delta_i^t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) is the number of samples assigned to item _i_. Let _N<sub>i</sub>(t_) denote the total samples allocated to item _i_ up to but not including round _t_, so that _N<sub>i</sub>_(0)=0, _N<sub>i</sub>_(1)=_n_<sub>0</sub>, and

\(N_i(t+1)=N_i(t)+\Delta_i^t,t=1,\dots,T.\)

Let H_<sub>t</sub>_ denote the history at time _t_, which is the collection of priors \(\{\Pi_{i,0}\}_{i=1}^I\) and observations \(\{Y_{i,n}:1\le i\le I\), \(1\le n\le N_i(t)\}\). We write \(\mathbb{E}_t[\cdot]\) and \(\mathbb{P}_t(\cdot)\) for conditional expectation and probability given H_<sub>t</sub>_. Let \(\Pi_{i,t}\) denote the posterior distribution of \(\theta_i\) given H_<sub>t</sub>_ and define \(\mu_i(t):=\mathbb{E}_t[\theta_i],v_i(t):=\mathbb{V}_t(\theta_i),F_{i,t}(x):=\mathbb{P}_t(\theta_i\le x)\). In round _t_, we refer to \(\Pi_{i,t}\) as the current prior.

In any round _t_, if we were to select items based on the current prior, we would pick the _k_ items with the largest posterior means. Thus, it is convenient to define the following: for any vector \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^I\), let _S<sub>k</sub>_(**x**) denote the set of indices of the _k_ largest elements of **x**. Write \(\mu(t)=(\mu_1(t),\dots,\mu_I(t))\) and \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_I)\). For any \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^I\), the opportunity cost of the current selection \(S_k(\mu(t))\) is<tbc>

\(\mathrm{OC}(S_k(\mu(t)),\theta):=\sum_{i\in S_k(\theta)}\theta_i-\sum_{i\in S_k(\mu(t))}\theta_i.\)

<tbc>Thus the Bayesian expected opportunity cost given H_<sub>t</sub>_ is

\(\mathrm{EOC}(\mathcal{H}_t)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta|\mathcal{H}_t}\big[\mathrm{OC}(S_k(\mu(t)),\theta)\big].\) (1)

The decision maker’s problem is to sequentially choose the sample batches \(\{\Delta^t\}_{t=1}^T\) that minimize the terminal expected opportunity cost EOC(H<sub>_T_+1</sub>). This can be formulated as a dynamic program, but it is intractable to solve, as discussed in the introduction. We next formulate a _static_ surrogate objective that guides the choice of batch in each round.

## 3. Surrogate objective via EOC bound

EOC(H_<sub>t</sub>_) does not generally admit an expression amenable to analysis, so (1) is not immediately useful for choosing which batch of samples to collect. Thus, we construct the per-round surrogate objective in two steps. First, Lemma 1 gives an upper bound on EOC(H_<sub>t</sub>_) that is amenable to analysis. Second, in §3.1, we make this bound a function of the round-_t_ allocation to guide the choice of future samples. We then discuss how<tbc>

<tbc>the resulting per-round objective differs from those in prior work in §3.2 and give efficient algorithms for finding the batch that minimizes it in §3.3. §3.4 presents the sequential sampling procedure, and §3.5 gives explicit expressions of the sampling rule for the ESCP. We begin with the EOC upper bound, which is based on comparing each item’s \(\theta_i\) to a threshold.

LEMMA 1 (Threshold upper bound on EOC).

(i) _For every threshold_ \(q\in\mathbb{R}\),<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathrm{EOC}(\mathcal{H}_t)\le\mathbb{E}_t\left[\sum_{i\in S_k(\mu(t))}(q-\theta_i)^++\sum_{i\notin S_k(\mu(t))}(\theta_i-q)^+\right].\)<tbc>

<tbc>(ii) _The right-hand side of_ (i) _is convex in q and has a unique minimizer q_<sup>∗</sup>(_t_) _characterized by_

\(\mathbb{E}_t\left[|\{i:\theta_i\ge q^*(t)\}|\right]=\sum_{i=1}^I\{1-F_{i,t}(q^*(t))\}=k.\) (2)

_Proof_ All proofs are provided in the Appendix.

Part (i) gives a family of upper bounds on EOC, each separable across items. For an item in the current top-_k_ set, its corresponding term in the bound is the expected shortfall of its true mean below threshold _q_. For an item outside this set, its corresponding term is the expected amount its true mean exceeds the threshold. Part (ii) states that the tightest bound in this family is given by _q_<sup>∗</sup>(_t_), the threshold such that, in expectation, exactly _k_ item means are larger than it. This makes _q_<sup>∗</sup>(_t_) a natural threshold choice when constructing the surrogate objective. We also consider another top-_k_ threshold motivated by the theoretical analysis in §4. Write \(d_i(x,y):=\mathrm{KL}(P_i(\cdot|x)\|P_i(\cdot|y))\) for the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the sampling distributions of item _i_ at means _x_ and _y_, and let \(\mu_{[1]}(t)\ge\cdots\ge\mu_{[I]}(t)\) denote the ordered posterior means. We define the threshold

\(q^\dagger(t):=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{argmin}_{\mu_{[k+1]}(t)<q<\mu_{[k]}(t)}\sum_{i=1}^I\frac{1}{d_i(\mu_i(t),q)}, & \mu_{[k]}(t)>\mu_{[k+1]}(t), \\
\mu_{[k]}(t), & \mu_{[k]}(t)=\mu_{[k+1]}(t).
\end{array}\right.\) (3)

§4 explains why this choice of top-_k_ threshold is "good". In what follows, let _q(t_) denote the top-_k_ threshold used in round _t_, which can be either _q_<sup>∗</sup>(_t_) or _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_).

## 3.1. Forward-looking objective

Given _q(t_), the threshold bound at state H_<sub>t</sub>_ is

\(\mathbb{E}_t\left[\sum_{i\in S_k(\mu(t))}(q(t)-\theta_i)^++\sum_{i\notin S_k(\mu(t))}(\theta_i-q(t))^+\right].\) (4)

To make this a function of a proposed round-_t_ allocation \(\unknown=(\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_I)\), we take the expectation with respect to an approximation of the random posterior of \(\theta_i\) _after_ allocating \(\unknown\) and observing its outcomes. This approximation preserves the shape of \(\Pi_{i,t}\) and has mean and variance equal to the expected posterior mean and variance. We say two distributions have the same _shape_ if they are equivalent after centering by their<tbc>

mean and scaling by their standard deviation. Put together, these conditions say that we replace the random future posterior with a deterministic, "shrunken" copy of the current prior, as it has the same mean as the prior, keeps the same shape, and changes only through a contraction around its mean by the expected amount of uncertainty that the proposed samples will remove. Figure 1 gives an example. Formally, we replace each \(\theta_i\) in (4) by the random variable \(\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i)\) that satisfies (i) \(\frac{\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i)-\mathbb{E}_t[\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i)]}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}_t(\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i))}}=^d\frac{\theta_i-\mu_i(t)}{\sqrt{v_i(t)}},\) (ii) \(\mathbb{E}_t[\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i)]=\mathbb{E}[\mu_i(t+1)|\Delta,\mathcal{H}_t]=\mu_i(t),\) (iii) \(\mathbb{V}_t(\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i))=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{V}(\theta_i|\mathcal{H}_{t+1})|\Delta,\mathcal{H}_t]=:\bar{v}_i(t,\Delta_i).\) For a given H_t_, this distribution is unique and is given by \(\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i)=\mu_i(t)+c_i(t,\Delta_i)(\theta_i-\mu_i(t)),c_i(t,\Delta_i):=\sqrt{\frac{\bar{v}_i(t,\Delta_i)}{v_i(t)}}.\) (5) We then define the surrogate loss induced by the allocation \(\Delta\) as \(\mathcal{L}_t(\Delta):=\mathbb{E}_t\left[\sum_{i\in S_k(\mu(t))}(q(t)-\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i))^++\sum_{i\notin S_k(\mu(t))}(\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i)-q(t))^+\right]\)
\(=\sum_{i=1}^I\mathbb{E}_t[(q(t)-\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i))^+]+\sum_{i\notin S_k(\mu(t))}(\mu_i(t)-q(t)),\) (6) where the second equality follows from (_x-q_)+=(_x-q_)+(_q-x_)+. The second sum is constant with respect to \(\Delta\). For the first sum we have \(\ell_{i,t}(\Delta_i):=\mathbb{E}_t[(q(t)-\widetilde{\theta}_i(\Delta_i))^+]=c_i(t,\Delta_i)\mathbb{E}_t[(z_i(t,\Delta_i)-\theta_i)^+],\) (7) Gaussian (batch Bt = 10) Beta (batch Bt = 10) 1.2 A B C A B C A = 5 A = 4 A = 1 A = 6 A = 4 A = 0 4.0 1.0 0.8 2.0 q* (t) q* (t) 0.6 value 0.0 value 0.4 -2.0 0.2 0.0 current prior post-allocation (current) loss contribution (post-allocation) **Figure 1** Structure of the surrogate loss \(\mathcal{L}_t(\cdot)\) and allocation for _I_=3, _k_=1 using _q(t_)=_q_∗(_t_). \(min_{\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^I}\sum_{i=1}^I\ell_{i,t}(\Delta_i)\text{s.t.}\sum_{i=1}^I\Delta_i=B_t,\) (8)

which is the per-round surrogate program. Conceptually, allocating according to (8) sends samples to the items whose posterior has substantial mass on both sides of the top-_k_ threshold _q(t_), weighted by the distance of that mass from _q(t_). These are the items whose membership in the top-_k_ set is uncertain and whose misclassification, if it occurs, could be costly.

## 3.2. Relation to OCBA-style objectives

Before analyzing how to solve (8), we discuss how its structure differs from static objectives in the OCBA literature for EOC. These objectives often use an upper bound on EOC based on a sum of losses associated with pairwise misorderings. For example, for top-1 EOC with Gaussian samples, He et al. (2007) use<tbc>

\(\mathrm{EOC}(\mathcal{H}_t)\le\sum_{i\neq i_{(1)}}\mathbb{E}_t[(\theta_i-\theta_{i_{(1)}})^+].\)

<tbc>Gao and Chen (2015) give the following bound on top-_k frequentist_ EOC:

\(\mathrm{EOC}\le\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{i\notin\{i_{(1)},\dots,i_{(j)}\}}\sum_{n=1}^j(\mu_{i_{(n)}}(t)-\mu_i(t))\Phi\left(-\frac{\mu_{i_{(n)}}(t)-\mu_i(t)}{\sqrt{v_{i_{(n)}}(t)+v_i(t)}}\right),\)

where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF, and _i_<sub>(1)</sub>_,...,i_<sub>(_I_)</sub> order the items by their current posterior means. Their static objective is then based on driving this bound down. The potential issue with using such a bound is that the candidate top-_k_ items {_i_<sub>(1)</sub>_,...,i_<sub>(_k_)</sub>} are in far more terms in the sum than the non-top-_k_ items. For instance, when _k_=1, _i_<sub>(1)</sub> is in all _I_-1 terms, while all other items are only in one term. Thus, an objective based on such a bound may over-count the benefit of sampling the top items. Our bound avoids these pairwise terms by comparing each item to the same threshold _q(t_), resulting in a single term for each item regardless of whether or not it is in \(S_k(\mu(t))\). EOC-m systematically allocates more samples to items in the top-_k_, even items far above the top-_k_ boundary, which is likely one of the main factors driving our method’s improvement over EOC-m, which we demonstrate in §5.

## 3.3. Batch allocation algorithm

Although (8) is an integer program, its separability across items allows us to solve it efficiently by dynamic programming and, in some cases, using a greedy procedure. Both are standard techniques. The main technical result of this subsection is Proposition 2(ii)–(iii), which gives conditions on the posterior distributions under which the greedy procedure is optimal.

The dynamic programming procedure in Algorithm 1 has two phases. First, we compute \(\ell_{i,t}(d)\) for every item _i_ and candidate allocation _d_=0_,...,B<sub>t</sub>_. Second, for each _r_=1_,...,I_ and _b_=0_,...,B<sub>t</sub>_, we solve the<tbc>

subproblem of allocating exactly _b_ samples among the first _r_ items by forward induction, and then recover the optimal allocation by backtracking. Let _V<sub>r</sub>(b_) denote the minimum loss for this subproblem so that _V<sub>I</sub>(B<sub>t</sub>_) is the optimal value of (8).

1: **Precompute cost values:** for each _i_=1_,...,I_ and _d_=0_,...,B<sub>t</sub>_, compute \(\ell_{i,t}(d)\)

2: **Initialize:** set _V_<sub>0</sub>(0)=0 and \(V_0(b)=+\infty\) for \(b=1,\dots,B_t\)

3: **Solve subproblems:**

4: **for** _r_=1_,...,I_

5: **for** _b_=0_,...,B<sub>t</sub>_

6: Compute \(V_r(b)=min_{\Delta\in\{0,\dots,b\}}\{V_{r-1}(b-\Delta)+\ell_{r,t}(\Delta)\}\) and record an argmin \(\Delta_r^*(b)\)

7: **Recover the allocation:** set \(b\leftarrow B_t\)

9: Set \(\Delta_r^t=\Delta_r^*(b)\) and update \(b\leftarrow b-\Delta_r^t\)

## 4. Theoretical guarantees

The guarantees in §3 concern the optimization of the surrogate objective (8), not the performance of TEAk in reducing EOC. In this section, we give asymptotic performance guarantees for TEAk. We begin by showing that TEAk is consistent (EOC(H_<sub>t</sub>_) converges to zero) and then make additional distributional assumptions to obtain a much stronger result. In particular, with threshold _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_), we show that the asymptotic exponential rate at which EOC(H_<sub>t</sub>_) converges to zero, referred to as the posterior convergence rate, is at least half of the best rate achievable by any sequential sampling rule.

<tbc>Throughout this section, we fix a true mean vector \(\theta^0\in\mathcal{J}^I\). We write \(\mathbb{P}_{\theta^0}\) and \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta^0}\) for probability and expectation over observations generated from \(P_i(\cdot|\theta_i^0)\). All convergence statements hold \(\mathbb{P}_{\theta^0}\)-almost surely. Although the true means are fixed, EOC(H_<sub>t</sub>_) remains the Bayesian posterior expectation in (1). Our rate guarantees also hold for the posterior error probability \(\mathbb{P}_t(S_k(\theta)\neq S_k(\theta^0))\), the quantity studied in the _k_=1 analyses of Russo (2020), Qin et al. (2017), and Shang et al. (2020).

These posterior guarantees should not be confused with guarantees for the frequentist EOC \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta^0}[\mathrm{OC}(S_k(\mu(t)),\theta^0)]\) and the frequentist probability of incorrect selection \(\mathbb{P}_{\theta^0}(S_k(\mu(t))\neq S_k(\theta^0))\). The posterior quantities measure the EOC and posterior error probability _conditional_ on an observed history, while the frequentist quantities average over observation histories. This distinction matters for exponential-rate guarantees: a sampling rule that achieves the optimal posterior convergence rate need not achieve the corresponding frequentist rate. In fact, no single sampling rule can generally guarantee a constant fraction of the best exponential decay rate of the frequentist probability of incorrect selection (likewise frequentist expected opportunity cost) uniformly across problem instances (Goldberger 2026, Degenne 2023).

**4.1. Consistency**

PROPOSITION 4 (**Consistency**). _Run TEAk for infinitely many rounds with threshold q_<sup>∗</sup>(_t_) _or q_<sup>†</sup>(_t). For q_<sup>†</sup>(_t), assume that the minimum in_ (3) _is attained whenever_ \(\mu_{[k]}(t)>\mu_{[k+1]}(t)\)_. There is a set_ \(\Theta^*\subseteq\mathcal{J}^I\) _with prior probability one such that for every_ \(\theta^0\in\Theta^*\)_, the following hold as_ \(t\rightarrow\infty\):

(i) \(N_i(t)\rightarrow\infty\), \(\mu_i(t)\rightarrow\theta_i^0\)_, and_ \(v_i(t)\rightarrow 0\) _for every i._<tbc>

(ii) \(\mathrm{EOC}(\mathcal{H}_t)\rightarrow 0\).<tbc>

(iii) _If_ \(\theta_{[k]}^0>\theta_{[k+1]}^0\)_, then_ \(S_k(\mu(t))=S_k(\theta^0)\) _for all sufficiently large t._

Part (i) says that every item is sampled infinitely often, and consequently its posterior mean converges to the true mean, and its posterior variance to 0. Parts (ii) and (iii) then follow: the posterior EOC converges to 0 and, when the true top-_k_ gap is positive, there is a finite time after which \(S_k(\mu(t))=S_k(\theta^0)\).

**4.2. The optimal exponential rate**

For the remainder of this section, assume \(1\le B_t\le B\) for every _t_ where _B_ is a fixed positive integer, and assume \(\theta_1^0\ge\cdots\ge\theta_k^0>\theta_{k+1}^0\ge\cdots\ge\theta_I^0\). We next establish an upper bound on the posterior convergence rate that any sequential sampling rule can achieve, and characterize the sample allocation that attains this bound. This gives the benchmark against which we will evaluate TEAk. We rely on the general posterior large-deviation analysis of Russo (2020), which we then apply to our top-_k_ EOC objective. Accordingly, we follow the distributional assumptions of Russo (2020).

<tbc>ASSUMPTION 2 (Bounded exponential-family model). _In addition to Assumption 1,_ J=(_L,U_) _with_ \(-\infty<L<U<\infty\)_. For every item i, the likelihood has the form_<tbc>

\(p_i(y|x)=h_i(y)exp\{\eta_i(x)T_i(y)-A_i(\eta_i(x))\},x\in\mathcal{J},\)

<tbc>_where T<sub>i</sub> is strictly increasing and A<sub>i</sub> is twice differentiable. Write_ \(\mathcal{E}_i:=\eta_i(\mathcal{J})=(\underline{\eta_i},\overline{\eta_i})\)_, with_ \(-\infty<\underline{\eta_i}<\overline{\eta_i}<\infty\)_, and let_ \(\widetilde{\pi}_{i,0}\) _denote the prior density of_ \(\eta_i(\theta_i)\)_. We assume_

\(sup_{\eta\in\mathcal{E}_i}|A'_i(\eta)|<\infty,0<inf_{\eta\in\mathcal{E}_i}\widetilde{\pi}_{i,0}(\eta)\le sup_{\eta\in\mathcal{E}_i}\widetilde{\pi}_{i,0}(\eta)<\infty.\)

The boundedness assumptions are used in the posterior convergence analysis primarily to facilitate generality across this broad range of families. As Russo (2020, p. 1635) notes, "Analogous results are easily established for certain unbounded conjugate priors." All five ESCP in Remark 1 satisfy Assumption 2 when their priors are restricted and normalized to a bounded interval whose closure is contained in J.

The next result shows that the exponential decay rate of a posterior probability is determined by the empirical sampling proportions. Let \(\Delta_I:=\{w\in\mathbb{R}^I:w_i\ge 0,\sum_iw_i=1\}\), and define the empirical sampling proportions by \(\widehat{w}_i(t):=N_i(t)/\sum_jN_j(t)\) for \(t\ge 2\).

LEMMA 2 (Russo (2020, Proposition 5)). _Under any sequential sampling rule, for every nonempty open set_ \(O\subseteq\mathcal{J}^I\),<tbc>

\(-\frac{log\mathbb{P}_t(\theta\in O)}{\sum_iN_i(t)}-inf_{x\in O}\sum_{i=1}^I\widehat{w}_i(t)d_i(\theta_i^0,x_i)\longrightarrow 0.\) (11)

<tbc>To interpret the first term in (11), \(\{\theta\in O\}\) is the "bad" event whose probability we want to control. For top-_k_ selection, _O_ is the set of _alternative_ parameters: parameters whose top-_k_ set is different from \(S_k(\theta^0)\). Ignoring ties which have a posterior probability of zero, these are the parameters where some pair of items (_i,j_) satisfies \(i\le k<j\), and yet \(\theta_j>\theta_i\). Accordingly, define the alternative space

\(Alt(\theta^0):=\bigcup_{i\le k<j}\{x\in\mathcal{J}^I:x_j>x_i\}\)

so that \(\mathbb{P}_t(\theta\in Alt(\theta^0))=\mathbb{P}_t(S_k(\theta)\neq S_k(\theta^0))\). We will apply Lemma 2 with \(O=Alt(\theta^0)\). In the second term, for fixed sampling proportions **_w_**, the quantity \(\sum_iw_id_i(\theta_i^0,x_i)\) is the expected log-likelihood ratio per observation between the true parameter \(\theta^0\) and an alternative **_x_**. The infimum over _O_ therefore identifies the alternative parameter that this allocation provides the least evidence to distinguish from the true parameter. For \(w\in\Delta_I\), denote this infimum at \(O=Alt(\theta^0)\) by \(\Gamma(w;\theta^0)\). Lemma 3 characterizes its structure.

LEMMA 3 (Pairwise representation of \(\Gamma\)). _For every_ \(w\in\Delta_I\),

\(\Gamma(w;\theta^0):=inf_{x\in Alt(\theta^0)}\sum_{\ell=1}^Iw_\ell d_\ell(\theta_\ell^0,x_\ell)=min_{i\le k<j}min_{x\in[\theta_j^0,\theta_i^0]}\{w_id_i(\theta_i^0,x)+w_jd_j(\theta_j^0,x)\}.\) (12)

\(\Gamma^*(\theta^0):=max_{w\in\Delta_I}\Gamma(w;\theta^0).\) (13)

The next proposition establishes that \(\Gamma^*(\theta^0)\) is the optimal exponential decay rate of posterior EOC and that it is attained by any sampling rule whose empirical proportions converge to a maximizer of (13).

PROPOSITION 5 **(Optimal exponential rate of posterior EOC).**

(i) _The maximum in_ (13) _is attained, and_ \(0<\Gamma^*(\theta^0)<\infty\).<tbc>

(ii) _Every sampling rule satisfies_<tbc>

<tbc>\(limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}-\frac{logEOC(\mathcal{H}_t)}{\sum_iN_i(t)}\le\Gamma^*(\theta^0).\)<tbc>

\(lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}-\frac{logEOC(\mathcal{H}_t)}{\sum_iN_i(t)}=\Gamma^*(\theta^0).\)

## 4.3. The rate of TEAk

To determine the rate TEAk achieves, it is sufficient to characterize the sample proportions produced asymptotically. First, we do this assuming the threshold _q(t_) converges to some point \(q\in(\theta_{k+1}^0,\theta_k^0)\). For such a _q_, define the proportions

\(w_i(q):=\frac{1/d_i(\theta_i^0,q)}{\sum_{j=1}^I1/d_j(\theta_j^0,q)},i=1,\dots,I.\) (14)

THEOREM 1 **(Allocation and rate for a convergent threshold)**. _Assume_ \(q(t)\rightarrow q_0\in(\theta_{k+1}^0,\theta_k^0)\)_. Then_

(i) \(\widehat{w}_i(t)\rightarrow w_i(q_0)\) _for every i,_<tbc>

(ii) \(-\frac{logEOC(\mathcal{H}_t)}{\sum_iN_i(t)}\rightarrow\Gamma(w(q_0);\theta^0)\),<tbc>

(iii) \(\Gamma(w(q_0);\theta^0)\ge\left(\sum_{i=1}^I1/d_i(\theta_i^0,q_0)\right)^{-1}\).

Part (i) says that the asymptotic sampling proportions of TEAk are described by (14). To prove this, we show that<tbc>

\(-\frac{logD_{i,t}(d)}{N_i(t)}\longrightarrow d_i(\theta_i^0,q_0)\text{for every}i\text{and}d=0,\dots,B-1.\)

<tbc>Thus, \(d_i(\theta_i^0,q_0)\) gives the exponential decay rate of the marginal decrease in the surrogate per sample of item _i_. Since TEAk allocates samples to the items with the largest marginal decreases (the argument under DPBB is a bit more technical but also holds), it asymptotically samples the items with the smallest \(N_i(t)d_i(\theta_i^0,q_0)\), which leads to balancing \(N_i(t)d_i(\theta_i^0,q_0)\) across all items. Therefore, the sampling proportions converge to _w<sub>i</sub>(q_<sub>0</sub>), which makes \(w_i(q_0)d_i(\theta_i^0,q_0)\) equal across items. Part (ii) says that TEAk’s posterior convergence<tbc>

<tbc>rate is then obtained by plugging these proportions into \(\Gamma\). Part (iii) gives a lower bound on TEAk’s rate, and we establish the one-half guarantee by comparing this lower bound, rather than \(\Gamma(w(q_0);\theta^0)\) itself, with the optimal rate \(\Gamma^*(\theta^0)\). This lower bound motivates choosing the threshold that makes it tightest,

\(q^\dagger\in argmin_{\theta_{k+1}^0<q<\theta_k^0}\sum_{i=1}^I\frac{1}{d_i(\theta_i^0,q)}.\)

Replacing the true means with the posterior means results in our choice of threshold _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_) in (3). This parallels our earlier choice of _q_<sup>∗</sup>(_t_): there we minimize an upper bound on the current EOC, whereas here we maximize a lower bound on its exponential decay rate.

It remains to show that \(q^\dagger(t)\rightarrow q^\dagger\). To establish this convergence, we assume the minimizer is unique.

ASSUMPTION 3 (**Unique threshold**). _For every_ \(x\in\mathcal{J}^I\) _with x_<sub>\[_k_\]</sub>_\>x_<sub>\[_k_+1\]</sub>_, the function_ \(q\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^I1/d_i(x_i,q)\) _has a unique minimizer on_ (_x_<sub>\[_k_+1\]</sub>_,x_<sub>\[_k_\]</sub>).

REMARK 3. _Each likelihood family in Remark 1 satisfies Assumption 3._

LEMMA 4 (**Convergence of** _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_)**)**.** _Run Algorithm 3 with threshold q_<sup>†</sup>(_t). Then_ \(q^\dagger(t)\rightarrow q^\dagger\).

By Lemma 4, Theorem 1 applies with _q_<sub>0</sub>=_q_<sup>†</sup>. We further show that \(\left(\sum_{i=1}^I1/d_i(\theta_i^0,q^\dagger)\right)^{-1}\ge\Gamma^*(\theta^0)/2\), which yields our main theoretical result.

THEOREM 2 (**Exponential rate of TEAk**). _Run Algorithm 3 with threshold q_<sup>†</sup>(_t). Then_

\(lim_{t\rightarrow\infty}-\frac{logEOC(\mathcal{H}_t)}{\sum_iN_i(t)}\ge\frac{1}{2}\Gamma^*(\theta^0).\)

Thus, the posterior convergence rate of TEAk is at least half the optimal posterior convergence rate. The conclusions in Proposition 5 and in Theorems 1 and 2 also hold when EOC(H_<sub>t</sub>_) is replaced by the posterior error probability \(\mathbb{P}_t(S_k(\theta)\neq S_k(\theta^0))\).

## 6. Discussion

We give a simple and interpretable algorithm for top-_k_ selection that accommodates batching in a principled way and can be applied to a wide range of sampling distribution families. We prove that it is consistent and that with the threshold _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_), its posterior convergence rate is at least half of the best rate achievable by any sampling rule. In simulation, it is competitive with the state-of-the-art methods across likelihood families, problem sizes, values of _k_, and batch sizes.

\(\frac{1}{d_i(x_i,e^z)}=\frac{2\sigma_i^2}{(logx_i-z)^2},\frac{d^2}{dz^2}\frac{1}{d_i(x_i,e^z)}=\frac{12\sigma_i^2}{(logx_i-z)^4}>0.\)

<tbc>For Bernoulli observations, write _q=e<sup>z</sup>/_(1+_e<sup>z</sup>_). We show that 1_/d<sub>i</sub>(x<sub>i</sub>,q_) is strictly convex in _z_. Differentiating gives<tbc>

\(\frac{d^2}{dz^2}\frac{1}{d_i(x_i,q)}=\frac{2(q-x_i)^2-d_i(x_i,q)q(1-q)}{d_i(x_i,q)^3}.\)

<tbc>To show that the numerator is positive, we bound _d<sub>i</sub>(x<sub>i</sub>,q_) from above. Using \(logu\le u-1\),<tbc>

\(d_i(x_i,q)=x_ilog\frac{x_i}{q}+(1-x_i)log\frac{1-x_i}{1-q}\le x_i\left(\frac{x_i}{q}-1\right)+(1-x_i)\left(\frac{1-x_i}{1-q}-1\right)=\frac{(x_i-q)^2}{q(1-q)}.\)

<tbc>Substituting gives

\(\frac{d^2}{dz^2}\frac{1}{d_i(x_i,q)}\ge\frac{(q-x_i)^2}{d_i(x_i,q)^3}>0,\)

since \(q\in(x_{[k+1]},x_{[k]})\) implies \(q\neq x_i\).

<tbc>For Poisson and Gamma observations, write _q=e<sup>z</sup>_. Then<tbc>

\(d_i(x_i,q)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
x_i(e^\nu-1-v), & v=z-logx_i,\text{Poisson}, \\
\kappa_i(e^\nu-1-v), & v=logx_i-z,\text{Gamma}.
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>Since \(x_i,\kappa_i>0\) and \(dv/dz=\pm 1\), it suffices to show that 1/(_e<sup>v</sup>_-1-_v_) is strictly convex for \(v\neq 0\). Differentiating gives<tbc>

\(\frac{d^2}{dv^2}\frac{1}{e^\nu-1-v}=\frac{e^\nu(e^\nu+2e^{-v}+v-3)}{(e^\nu-1-v)^3}.\)

<tbc>The denominator is positive for \(v\neq 0\). To show that the numerator is positive, use _e<sup>v</sup>\>_1+_v_ and _e_<sup>-_v_</sup>_\>_1-_v_ to get

\(e^\nu+2e^{-v}+v-3>(1+v)+2(1-v)+v-3=0.\)

Thus the second derivative is positive, proving strict convexity in _z_ for both families. \(\square\)

_Proof of Lemma 4_ By Lemma 9 and the proof of Lemma 7, \(\unknown(t)\rightarrow\unknown^0\). Define

\(H_t(q):=\sum_i\frac{1}{d_i(\mu_i(t),q)},H(q):=\sum_i\frac{1}{d_i(\theta_i^0,q)}.\)

We will show that every limit of _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_) belongs to \((\theta_{k+1}^0,\theta_k^0)\) and minimizes _H_. Uniqueness then gives convergence to _q_<sup>†</sup>.

Since \(\mu_{[k]}(t)\rightarrow\theta_k^0\) and \(\mu_{[k+1]}(t)\rightarrow\theta_{k+1}^0\), eventually \(\mu_{[k+1]}(t)<q^\dagger<\mu_{[k]}(t)\). Since _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_) minimizes _H<sub>t</sub>_ on this interval,<tbc>

\(H_t(q^\dagger(t))\le H_t(q^\dagger)\longrightarrow H(q^\dagger)<\infty.\) (26)

<tbc>Let \(t_n\rightarrow\infty\) satisfy \(q^\dagger(t_n)\rightarrow\bar{q}\). Since \(\mu_{[k+1]}(t)\le q^\dagger(t)\le\mu_{[k]}(t)\), we have \(\bar{q}\in[\theta_{k+1}^0,\theta_k^0]\). If \(\bar{q}=\theta_k^0\) (and likewise \(\bar{q}=\theta_{k+1}^0\)), then<tbc>

\(H_{t_n}(q^\dagger(t_n))\ge\frac{1}{d_k(\mu_k(t_n),q^\dagger(t_n))}\longrightarrow\infty,\)

<tbc>contradicting (26). Therefore \(\bar{q}\in(\theta_{k+1}^0,\theta_k^0)\), and continuity gives

\(H(\bar{q})=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} H_{t_n}(q^\dagger(t_n))\le H(q^\dagger).\)

Thus \(\bar{q}\) minimizes _H_, and Assumption 3 gives \(\bar{q}=q^\dagger\). Since _q_<sup>†</sup>(_t_) is eventually contained in a compact interval and every such limit equals _q_<sup>†</sup>, we conclude that \(q^\dagger(t)\rightarrow q^\dagger\). \(\square\)

_Proof of Theorem 2_ By Lemma 4 and Theorem 1(ii),<tbc>

\(-\frac{logEOC(\mathcal{H}_t)}{\sum_iN_i(t)}\longrightarrow\Gamma(w(q^\dagger);\unknown^0)\le\Gamma^*(\unknown^0).\)

<tbc>For the lower bound, write \(H(q):=\sum_i1/d_i(\theta_i^0,q)\). Part (iii) of Theorem 1 gives

\(\Gamma(w(q^\dagger);\unknown^0)\ge\frac{1}{H(q^\dagger)}.\)

It therefore remains to show \(\Gamma^*(\unknown^0)/2\le 1/H(q^\dagger)\).

<tbc>Let **_w_**<sup>∗</sup> maximize \(\Gamma\). By the proof of Proposition 5, \(w_i^*>0\) for every _i_. The functions (of _q_)

\(min_{i\le k}w_i^*d_i(\theta_i^0,q),min_{j>k}w_j^*d_j(\theta_j^0,q)\)

are continuous on \([\theta_{k+1}^0,\theta_k^0]\). The first is positive at \(\theta_{k+1}^0\) and zero at \(\theta_k^0\), while the second is zero at \(\theta_{k+1}^0\) and positive at \(\theta_k^0\). Thus they are equal at some \(\bar{q}\in(\theta_{k+1}^0,\theta_k^0)\). Write

\(r:=min_{i\le k}w_i^*d_i(\theta_i^0,\bar{q})=min_{j>k}w_j^*d_j(\theta_j^0,\bar{q})>0.\)

Choose \(i\le k<j\) attaining the two minima. Evaluating (12) at this pair and \(x=\bar{q}\) gives

\(\Gamma^*(\theta^0)\le w_i^*d_i(\theta_i^0,\bar{q})+w_j^*d_j(\theta_j^0,\bar{q})=2r.\)

Since \(w_i^*d_i(\theta_i^0,\bar{q})\ge r\) for every _i_,

\(rH(\bar{q})=\sum_i\frac{r}{d_i(\theta_i^0,\bar{q})}\le\sum_iw_i^*=1.\)

Since _q_<sup>†</sup> minimizes _H_,

\(\frac{1}{2}\Gamma^*(\theta^0)\le r\le\frac{1}{H(\bar{q})}\le\frac{1}{H(q^\dagger)}\le\Gamma(w(q^\dagger);\theta^0).\)

The corresponding result for the posterior error follows from Lemma 8. \(\square\)
